sections.title: Adding symbols
content: Click any arrow (connector) in the flowchart: a symbol picker opens, and the symbol you pick is inserted there.
The new symbol opens for editing right away. In every dialog, Enter presses the default (blue) button, e.g. Save or OK; Esc closes the dialog.

sections.title: Editing and deleting
content: Click a symbol to edit it. Use the Delete button in its editor to remove it.

sections.title: Undo and redo
content: In the header, between Save and Export Image, are the Undo button (the arrow curving back) and, next to it, Redo. Undo brings back the previous state of the flowchart, and it goes back many steps — all the way to how the program looked when it was opened. Keyboard: Ctrl+Z.

Redo undoes the undo. It only becomes active once you have undone something. Keyboard: Ctrl+Y (or Ctrl+Shift+Z). If you start editing again after an undo, the undone steps are gone and Redo goes grey again.

Undo covers the whole program: symbols, procedures, structs, comments and breakpoints, on whichever tab you edited them. Starting a new program, opening one or loading an example begins with an empty history, and stops a running program.

sections.title: Right-click menu, cut and paste
content: Right-click a symbol for its menu: edit, cut, add a comment (to the selection, if the symbol is selected), set or remove a breakpoint, delete.
Cut takes the symbol out (an If or loop moves together with everything inside it). A badge in the header shows what was cut.
Right-click an arrow to paste it there. With nothing cut, the symbol picker opens instead.
Click the badge in the header to discard the cut symbol (it is then lost).

sections.title: Selecting, collapsing, commenting
content: Selecting: drag a rectangle with the right mouse button on an empty area – every symbol it touches gets selected, and the menu opens when you release the button. Ctrl + click selects too (Ctrl + click again to deselect). Dragging with the left button still scrolls the canvas; Esc or clicking an empty area clears the selection.

Collapse…: chosen from the menu, it opens a small dialog. The comment (the section's name) is filled in, e.g. "3 symbols", and selected, so you can type over it at once, e.g. "Here we declared three variables". "Collapsed" is ticked: Enter collapses the section at once. A single symbol's right-click menu has it too.

The comment stands on a note at the start of the section, with a round − button below it, and another one at the end, labelled "end: …". Click − to collapse the section (like #region in C#): the note shows as a stack, with a round + button and "3 symbols hidden" below it; click + to expand it again.
Click the note to edit the comment; right-click it to collapse, expand, remove the comment (the symbols stay) or delete the whole section.
A collapsed section runs exactly as its symbols would. In the generated code it is a comment (in C#, a #region).
An example to try: the "Comments, collapsible sections" program in the Basics group of the New dialog.

sections.title: View
content: Use the bottom-right controls to zoom in (+), zoom out (−) or fit the whole diagram (⛶). Drag the empty background to scroll. Drag the divider between the diagram and the side panel to set the panel width — this browser remembers it. Dialogs can be moved by dragging their title bar (or any empty part of them).

Settings: click the wrench at the top right to choose the language and to set the size of the whole app in percent (− and + shrink and enlarge it at once; the browser remembers it). It also shows the version and which edition you use (web, exam or offline with examples), and opens the download page.

sections.title: Procedures and functions
content: Use the "+ Routine" tab to create a procedure or function with parameters; edit it with the ✎ icon. Call it with a Call symbol or from an expression, e.g. Double(n).

A function's return value is the value that the variable named after the function holds when the function ends. A parameter marked "by reference" changes the caller's variable; arrays are always passed by reference.

sections.title: Structs (records)
content: Use "+ Struct" to create your own type with a name and fields (e.g. Point: x, y). A field can be of a basic type or another struct. Click a struct's tab to edit, rename or delete it.

A struct can be chosen anywhere a type is: in Declare (also as an array), for parameters and as a function's return type. Access fields with a dot: p.x, t[i].name, r.corner.x — in expressions, assignments and Input.

A struct can get all its fields at once: in Assign, enter the struct variable (e.g. p), tick "All fields at once" and fill in the fields. It is saved as one assignment per field, together in a collapsed commented section ("Assigning the fields of p").
Assignment (b = a) and by-value parameters copy the struct; a by-reference parameter changes the original.

sections.title: Files
content: On the Files tab you can upload files, create new ones, view and edit their content, rename, download and delete them. Files are kept in this browser.
A program refers to a file by its name, as a String: "file-a". Symbols: Open File (for reading, writing or appending), Read from File (reads one line into a variable), Write to File, Close File.

eof("file-a") is true when a file open for reading has no more lines — e.g. a loop: while not eof("file-a"). Read, Write, Close and EOF() can omit the file name, in which case they use the most recently opened file (the way Flowgorithm handles files).
Opening a file for writing creates (or overwrites) it; what the program creates appears on the Files tab right away, ready to download.

sections.title: Running
content: ▶ Run executes the program. The symbol being executed is highlighted in blue: the Start symbol lights up first, and the End symbol lights up last, when the program has finished. Set the pace with the Speed selector.
⏸ Pause pauses the run; continue with ▶ or ⏭.
⟲ Reset starts over and clears the console and variables.
An Input symbol asks for a value on the Console tab; the program waits until you enter it.

sections.title: Stepping
content: The ⏭ Step button executes one symbol at a time. Follow the current variable values on the Variables tab and the output on the Console tab. You can switch to ▶ Run at any time.

sections.title: Debugging
content: Breakpoint: Shift + click a symbol, or select "Breakpoint" in its editor. A red dot in the corner of the symbol marks it.
During a run, the program stops at a breakpoint before executing that symbol, and switches to the Variables tab.
Variables changed by the last step are highlighted in yellow.
Continue step by step (⏭) or to the next breakpoint (▶).
Breakpoint symbol (as in Flowgorithm): the run stops when it gets there — with a condition (e.g. i = 4), only when the condition is true.
On a runtime error, the symbol that caused it is highlighted and the message appears in the console.

sections.title: Files, examples, source code
content: The Files tab manages the data files programs read and write (see Files).
Save: to a .flow file. Open: a .flow file, or a .fprg file made with Flowgorithm (anything the app doesn't support, e.g. turtle graphics, is reported). Your program is also kept in this browser.
Updates: when a new version of the app comes out, the page updates itself as soon as no program is running and no dialog is open — the open program and the view are kept.
The buttons in the header are icon-only (New, Open, Save, Export Image, then the run controls): hover over one to see which is which. Export Image makes a PNG image of the flowchart.

New: the dialog shown at start — an empty project or ready-made examples (examples from the Hungarian Digital Culture textbooks, algorithms, structs, files); a loaded example can be edited and extended as if you had written it.
The Code tab generates Python, C++ or C# source code from the program — highlighted, with line numbers; Enlarge shows it in a big window.

Pseudocode writes the program in the app's language: in English, the pseudocode of Cambridge International AS & A Level Computer Science (DECLARE, IF … THEN … ENDIF, FOR … NEXT, PROCEDURE, FUNCTION … RETURNS); in Hungarian, the mondatszerű leírás taught at ELTE. Arrays and strings are indexed from 0 here too, as in the flowchart.

sections.title: Expressions
content: Arrays: t[i], indexed from 0. Struct fields: p.x, t[i].name.
Strings in quotes: "apple" or 'apple' (no escape sequences; \ is an ordinary character).
Names (variables, routines) start with a letter and contain letters, digits and underscores; case doesn't matter.
The full list of operators and functions is in the tables below.

sections.title: Adding a language
content: Each language of the app is a JSON file in the languages/ folder of the public https://github.com/laszlorepassy/flowchart-languages repository, named after the language's code: de.json (German), fr.json (French), pt-BR.json (Brazilian Portuguese), and so on. The reference is languages/en.json (English); languages/hu.json is the Hungarian file. Anyone can add a new language or improve an existing one.
1. Sign in to GitHub, open the repository and fork it (the Fork button).
2. In your fork, copy languages/en.json to languages/<code>.json, e.g. languages/de.json. The code is the language's two-letter ISO 639-1 code, optionally followed by a region (pt-BR).

3. Fill in the "language" block: "code" (the file name without .json), "name" (the language's name in English), "nativeName" (its own name, shown in the settings' language choice) and "translators" (your name, shown at the bottom of the help).
4. Translate only the values (after the colon), never the keys (before the colon). You can edit on GitHub itself (the pencil icon) or in any text editor that saves files as UTF-8.
5. Send a pull request to the repository. The "Validate language files" check runs automatically and tells you exactly what is left to fix.
6. An accepted language appears in the next version of the web app and the desktop editions, in the settings and among the help's language buttons.
You don't have to translate everything at once: a message you leave out is shown in English, and without the "help" block the help is shown in English.
"messages" is the user interface: buttons, menus, error messages. Keep short texts short: buttons and tabs have little room.
Placeholders in curly braces, e.g. {name}, {expected}, {file}, are filled in by the app: keep each one exactly as it is, but put it wherever your language needs it in the sentence.

Code is not translated: the flowchart language's keywords and functions (and, or, not, mod, Len, ToString, eof…), the type names (Integer, Real, String, Boolean), examples written in them, file names and commands stay as they are.

"help" → "sections" is the help: every section has a "title" and either "content" (a string is a paragraph; a list of strings is a bulleted list) or a "table" (translate the head and the text cells, not the code columns listed in "codeColumns").

"help" → "examReplacements" and "offlineReplacements": in the exam edition and the offline edition, a help line starting with the text on the left is shown as the text on the right. Translate both so that the left side is exactly the start of your translated help line.
"help" → "download": the download page's texts for the exam edition's installers (with the {version} and {file} placeholders).

You can check the file on your own computer too, in the repository's folder: node tools/languages.mjs (needs Node.js 18 or newer), or with only Docker: docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/w -w /w node:20-alpine node tools/languages.mjs. ERROR lines must be fixed; note lines only list what is still in English.
The built-in example programs and the pseudocode view exist in English and Hungarian only; in other languages they are shown in English.
